All polyharmonic functions in the unit disk can be described by means of trigonometric series. This representation provides a systematic way to express such functions in terms of their angular components and radial behavior. By expanding the functions into Fourier-type series, one obtains a clear analytic framework for studying their structure and properties inside the disk.

A central question is whether these polyharmonic functions possess boundary values on the unit circle. The theory establishes that such boundary values do indeed exist. As the points inside the disk approach the boundary, the corresponding limiting objects can be meaningfully defined, even when classical pointwise or distributional limits may not exist.

More precisely, the boundary values are shown to exist in the space of hyperfunctions. Hyperfunctions provide a very general setting for boundary value problems, extending the notions of functions and distributions. This makes it possible to assign boundary values to a broad class of polyharmonic functions, including cases where the behavior near the boundary is too singular for more restrictive function spaces.

Finally, the theory gives necessary and sufficient conditions that determine when these boundary values belong to particular subspaces of hyperfunctions. These criteria connect the growth and coefficient behavior of the trigonometric series representation with the regularity of the resulting boundary values. In this way, the classification of boundary values is made precise: one can decide exactly when a polyharmonic function has boundary values not only as hyperfunctions in general, but also in more refined spaces such as distributions, ultradistributions, or other distinguished subspaces.

This text investigates the boundary behavior of polyharmonic functions defined in the unit disk. A function is called polyharmonic of order \(m\) if it is annihilated by the \(m\)-th power of the Laplace operator, that is,
\[
\Delta^m u = 0.
\]
Such functions generalize harmonic functions and arise naturally in potential theory, partial differential equations, and complex analysis. In the unit disk, polyharmonic functions admit representations in terms of trigonometric series, generalizing the classical Fourier expansion of harmonic functions.

The main focus is on describing how these trigonometric series behave as the radius approaches the boundary of the disk. For harmonic functions, boundary values are often studied in terms of functions, distributions, or measures on the unit circle. For polyharmonic functions, the situation is more delicate, because the higher-order Laplace equation allows more complicated radial behavior. The text therefore studies boundary values in the broader framework of hyperfunctions.

Hyperfunctions provide a natural setting for describing generalized boundary values. They contain distributions as a proper subspace and are flexible enough to capture boundary limits of analytic or harmonic objects that may fail to converge in the usual function or distributional sense. The text proves that every polyharmonic function in the unit disk possesses a boundary value on the unit circle in the sense of hyperfunctions. This boundary value is obtained through the asymptotic behavior of the trigonometric expansion as the point approaches the unit circle from inside the disk.

More precisely, the polyharmonic function is represented by a series involving angular Fourier modes and radial factors determined by the order of polyharmonicity. By analyzing the growth of the Fourier coefficients and their dependence on the radial variable, the text identifies the corresponding hyperfunction on the boundary. This establishes a precise correspondence between polyharmonic functions in the disk and certain hyperfunctions on the unit circle.

The text then goes further and characterizes when the boundary value belongs to particular subspaces of the space of hyperfunctions. These subspaces may include distributions, ultradistributions, or other classes determined by prescribed growth conditions on Fourier coefficients. The result is expressed through necessary and sufficient conditions: a polyharmonic function has a boundary value in a given hyperfunction subspace if and only if its trigonometric-series coefficients satisfy the corresponding growth or decay estimates.

Thus, the work gives a complete description of boundary values of polyharmonic functions in terms of Fourier coefficients. It shows not only that hyperfunction boundary values always exist, but also precisely determines the regularity class of those boundary values. In this way, the text extends classical boundary-value theory for harmonic functions to the broader setting of polyharmonic functions and hyperfunction analysis on the unit circle.

**For** and **the** are two of the most common words in English, yet they play very different roles.

**The** is a definite article. It is used when we are talking about something specific or already known. For example, in the phrase “the book,” we mean a particular book, not just any book.

**For** is a preposition that can show purpose, reason, benefit, or duration. For example, “This gift is for you” shows benefit, while “I studied for three hours” shows duration.

Together, these small words help make sentences clearer and more precise. Although they are simple, **for** and **the** are essential parts of everyday communication.

For a function satisfying \(\Delta^{m}u=0\) in the disk, the Almansi-type expansion yields Fourier coefficients with controlled radial dependence, leading to a representation by finite sums of powers of \(1-r^{2}\) multiplied by harmonic components. We formulate necessary and sufficient conditions on the associated trigonometric series so that it determines a polyharmonic function with prescribed boundary behavior. The boundary values are interpreted in the space of hyperfunctions on the unit circle, allowing coefficients with growth beyond the distributional setting. This framework identifies polyharmonic functions as Poisson-type extensions of hyperfunction boundary data together with higher-order boundary traces, and it clarifies the correspondence between radial coefficient estimates, convergence in the disk, and hyperfunction boundary convergence. The result provides a natural extension of classical harmonic Fourier theory to higher-order elliptic equations and generalized boundary spaces.
